rat-removal.intro: Cross is a Berkeley County community in the Lake Moultrie country — a rural crossroads settlement of farms, older homes, and fish-camp country near the lake's north shore, where rats are a farm building problem before they are a house problem. Norway rats burrow along the barn foundations, the feed rooms, and the lake-side outbuildings, and roof rats work the palms and the older homes' rooflines nearer the water. The calls come when the burrow system reaches the house — rats in the crawlspace, in the walls, at the pet food — but the population that matters is usually anchored at the feed: grain, pet food, and the lake camps' bins. Rat work in Cross is population work, and it starts with the food map.
rat-removal.extendedBody:
Feed first, then the burrows

A Cross rat job is sequenced honestly: the food, the burrows, the building. We map where the rats are eating — feed storage, bins, pet food, the camp kitchens — because a trapped population with its pantry intact is replaced from the surrounding ground within weeks, while a population whose food is sealed into metal bins has a ceiling the trapping can actually reach. Then the burrow systems along the foundations are worked, and the house itself is sealed: crawlspace vents, pipe penetrations, the gaps at the slab. We do not scatter poison as a programme — around feed, stock, dogs, and a lake, broadcast rodenticide is a hazard traded for a result it rarely delivers, and the owls and hawks that hunt Cross's rat population are worth more alive than any bait station. Trapping, exclusion, and food discipline is slower to describe and faster to finish: it is the version whose results are still there in the next season.

faqs.q: How much does rat removal cost in Cross?
faqs.a: It depends on the anchor — a house-only problem with one burrow line is one job; a farm population anchored at the feed room, with burrows at the barn and the house, is a programme. We survey the property's food map and burrows first and quote the whole sequence — trapping, burrow work, and building sealing — as one firm price. If the honest first step is bins and feed storage, we will say so and price the programme around it, rather than trap expensively into a stocked pantry.

faqs.q: Why won't you just put out poison for our Cross rat problem?
faqs.a: Because around feed, animals, and water it trades one problem for worse ones and usually fails anyway. Rats that die in walls and burrows become a dead-animal problem; poisoned rats eaten by the owls, hawks, and dogs of the neighbourhood kill the very predators that hold the population down between our visits; and a colony with open food replaces its losses faster than bait removes them. Trapping on the burrow systems, sealing the building, and putting the feed into metal is the method that ends Cross rat problems, and its results do not wash into Lake Moultrie.
